message.content:
We don’t have a definitive “largest planet” in the entire universe—our knowledge is limited to what we’ve observed so far. Among the planets we’ve discovered outside our Solar System (exoplanets), the biggest ones are often called “super‑Jupiters.” Some of the most massive and largest exoplanets we know include:

| Exoplanet | Approximate Mass | Approximate Radius |
|-----------|------------------|--------------------|
| **HD 100546 b** | ~20–30 M_J (Jupiter masses) | ~10–12 R_J |
| **WASP‑17b** | ~0.5 M_J | ~1.9 R_J (very low density) |
| **Kepler‑39b** | ~24 M_J | ~1.0 R_J |
| **KELT‑9b** | ~2.8 M_J | ~1.7 R_J |

These planets are among the largest we’ve confirmed, but there may well be larger ones out there that we haven’t yet detected. In practice, the size of a planet is constrained by its mass and composition; beyond a certain point, additional mass leads to gravitational compression rather than a larger radius. Thus, while we can identify the biggest known exoplanets, the true maximum size remains unknown until we discover more objects or develop better detection methods.
